hints: Compare what is left behind when phenol loses $\text{H}^+$ with what is left behind when water loses $\text{H}^+$, and think about which negative ion is more stable.
Think about where the lone pair on the oxygen atom in phenol can go, and how this affects the $\text{O-H}$ bond and the stability of the anion formed.
walkthrough:
Picture what acidity really means here**
Think of acidity as how easily a molecule lets go of $\text{H}^+$. For phenol: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^- + \text{H}^+$. For water: $\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{OH}^- + \text{H}^+$. The more stable the negative ion left behind, the further this equilibrium lies to the right.

See what the oxygen lone pair does in phenol**
In phenol the oxygen is directly attached to the benzene ring. One of its lone pairs sits in a p orbital that can overlap sideways with the delocalised pi system of the ring. So that lone pair is partly drawn into the ring. This pulls electron density away from oxygen and weakens the $\text{O-H}$ bond, making $\text{H}^+$ loss easier.

Compare the two anions**
In $\text{OH}^-$ the negative charge is stuck entirely on one small oxygen atom. In the phenoxide ion, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$, the negative charge on oxygen can also be delocalised into the ring. Spreading the charge over a larger volume stabilises the ion. A more stable conjugate base means a stronger acid, so phenol is more acidic than water.

Final answer: A lone pair in a p orbital on the O atom overlaps with / is delocalised into the benzene ring.
This weakens the $\text{O-H}$ bond in phenol and stabilises the phenoxide ion, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$, so phenol loses $\text{H}^+$ more readily than water.

hints: Recall how strongly the $\text{OH}$ group activates the benzene ring, and whether bromine water needs a catalyst or gives mono or tri substitution with phenol.
walkthrough:
Remember phenol with bromine water**
The $\text{OH}$ group is very strongly activating, so phenol is so reactive that even weak electrophiles attack without a catalyst. With excess $\text{Br}_2(aq)$, substitution happens at both ortho positions and the para position, giving the white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol. Each substitution releases $\text{HBr}$ as the second product.

hints: Use the $M_r = 139$ to work out how many $\text{NO}_2$ groups have added to phenol ($M_r = 94$), remembering that each nitration replaces one H with one $\text{NO}_2$.
walkthrough:
Check the mass to find the degree of nitration**
Phenol, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, has $M_r = 94$. Replacing H (1) by $\text{NO}_2$ (46) adds 45. $94 + 45 = 139$, so this is mononitration. Dilute $\text{HNO}_3(aq)$ at room temperature gives only one $\text{NO}_2$ group per ring.

Place the nitro group where OH directs**
$\text{OH}$ is ortho and para directing and very activating. So you get two isomers: $\text{NO}_2$ ortho to $\text{OH}$ to give 2-nitrophenol, and $\text{NO}_2$ para to $\text{OH}$ to give 4-nitrophenol. Draw a benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ at the top, then $\text{NO}_2$ at the adjacent carbon for the ortho isomer and at the opposite carbon for the para isomer.

Final answer: 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol: a benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ and one $\text{NO}_2$ group ortho to $\text{OH}$, and a benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ and one $\text{NO}_2$ group para to $\text{OH}$.

hints: Think of phenol behaving like an alcohol towards Na, with the acidic $\text{OH}$ proton replaced by Na and a gas evolved.
walkthrough:
Treat it like an acid plus metal reaction**
The $\text{O-H}$ proton is acidic enough to be displaced by sodium. Sodium takes the place of H to form sodium phenoxide, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa}$, and hydrogen gas bubbles off. Balance to give 2 phenol to 2 sodium to 2 phenoxide to 1 hydrogen: $$2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} + \text{H}_2$$

hints: Recall the standard way to convert a primary aromatic amine into a diazonium salt, including the nitrite reagent and the critical low temperature.
Think about what happens when a benzenediazonium salt is warmed in water, and what small molecules are lost to give the $\text{OH}$ group.
walkthrough:
Make the diazonium salt first**
Phenylamine, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$, cannot be turned directly into $\text{OH}$. First convert $\text{NH}_2$ into a good leaving group, the diazonium group $\text{N}_2^+$. Use sodium nitrite plus hydrochloric acid, which generates nitrous acid, $\text{HNO}_2$, in the mixture. This must be kept very cold, at or below $10^{\circ}\text{C}$, otherwise the diazonium salt, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$, decomposes.

Hydrolyse by warming in water**
Then warm the benzenediazonium chloride solution with water. Heating above $10^{\circ}\text{C}$ causes $\text{N}_2$ gas to be lost and $\text{OH}$ from water to take its place: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{N}_2 + \text{H}^+$$ This gives phenol directly.

Final answer: step one reagents: $\text{NaNO}_2$ + $\text{HCl}$ (to form $\text{HNO}_2$ in situ); conditions: $T \leqslant 10^{\circ}\text{C}$ (kept cold, ice bath).
step two reagents: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$; conditions: warm / heat / $T > 10^{\circ}\text{C}$.
